items.text:
The largest fleet of electric school buses in New York State is up and running in a South Bronx neighborhood where childhood asthma rates are more than twice the national average.
Family-owned school bus company GVC has served schoolchildren with special needs in the Bronx for more than 30 years, and the company worked over the summer to install 23 dual‑port chargers to power 45 new electric school buses.
The buses will collectively prevent the emission of 1 million pounds of emissions per school year. Exhaust pollutants like carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and fine particulate matter pose serious threats to residents’ long-term pulmonary health, including through elevated asthma risk, and those most at risk are passengers waiting for buses and sitting on buses—the schoolchildren included.
GVC’s bus depot is located on Zerega Avenue, along a 2-mile corridor where around 2,000 school buses and 3,000 medium and heavy-duty vehicles pass every day.
“The children we transport are especially vulnerable to air and noise pollution,” Michael Townsend, Compliance Officer at GVC, said in a statement.
“Transitioning our fleet to electric is making a difference in people’s lives. The children we transport, and all those who live and work in the area, are enjoying cleaner air and quieter streets.”
Con Edison, one of New York’s largest utilities, worked with GVC from the earliest stages of their bus fleet transition, upgrading the grid to handle the demand from the bus chargers, offering a $450,000 incentive , and identifying other avenues of support from the city and state governments that could accelerate the transition.
This included the New York School Bus Incentive Program (NYSBIP) funded by the Clean Water, Clean Air, and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act. The NYSBIP helped fund 20 of GVC’s electric buses and the 23 dual-port chargers.

“Con Edison is proud to invest in energy solutions that anticipate customers’ needs, reduce emissions, protect public health, and support New York’s clean energy transition,” said Vicki Kuo, Senior Vice President of Customer Energy Solutions, in a statement.
GVC’s electric buses will carry about 800 children to their classes, averaging 18 Early Intervention to Pre-Kindergarten students per ride. Over the course of a school week, the fleet serves an estimated 4,100 student trips.

Mayor Daniel Lurie joined Chesky for the announcement last week in Golden Gate Park.
Chesky founded Airbnb in San Francisco 18 years ago and the company is still headquartered there. For him, the donation is about “giving back to the city that made Airbnb possible”.
The new resources will speed up construction timelines, deliver upgrades and programming, and close funding gaps.
“San Francisco has nature, parks, beaches, and views that you can’t find anywhere else, with affordable recreation programs where a kid discovers a love of baseball, a teenager finds mentorship, and a working parent knows their children are safe after school,” said Mayor Lurie.
“San Francisco is one of the most beautiful cities in the world, and our parks are a big part of what makes it special,” said Chesky. “I’ve always believed in the power of bringing people together, and parks are where a city meets.”

“Public parks are not just patches of green; they are the social, physical, and backbone of our neighborhoods,” said District 7 Supervisor Myrna Melgar. “This investment is an extraordinary gift to San Francisco families.”
“I learned to fish at India Basin and went to softball tryouts at Garfield. items.text:
A new generation of trash bins are aimed at conserving Japanese civic culture while addressing one of the country’s largest tourism headaches.
Solar-powered compactors and robots that haul trash away from key tourist areas are two such solutions already receiving a positive response.
If you’ve ever visited Japan, you too may have been left confused and eventually frustrated by what appears to be a total absence of public waste bins. This is by design.
Officials concerned about security and overflowing bins have left the public with few places to dispose of their trash. There is also a philosophy that if waste is difficult to dispose of, people will be less prone to creating it.
Japanese tourism authorities are beginning to understand that, while this approach may have seen citizens keep their streets clean for decades, it’s a major inconvenience for visitors.
Yet the trend towards removing waste bins has continued, with the Tokyo metro removing all public waste bins as recently as 2022. In parallel, however, the city has been enlisting the help of various firms to design smarter waste bins that hold more and won’t overflow.
One example is Forcetec, which sells and installs solar-powered waste bins developed in the United States called SmaGO. It compacts waste every 5 minutes and can hold 5 times as much trash as a non-compacting bin.
“There are many places that recognize the need for trash bins but hesitate to install them because they’re worried the bins will overflow or because of the labor required to collect the rubbish,” says Rina Ogata, a spokesperson for Forcetec.
“You can install SmaGO and reduce the frequency of rubbish collection. The communications function also allows operators to check online how full each bin is, so they can make collections more efficiently before the bins reach capacity.”
Companies like Forcetec have donated or subsidized these products as part of “a corporate hometown tax program” and “corporate sponsorships” according to Japan Times .
Another reason why cities like Kyoto and Tokyo decided to trash their trash cans was that they fill up too quickly in busy areas, and collection of each bin was an expensive outlay.
But what if the trash cans could collect themselves? Enter California-based firm Cartken , whose 40-liter robotic trash bins use sensors to measure when they’re almost full, at which point they drive themselves out of the public reach for emptying.

items.text:
2 prominent chemical compounds prohibited under international law over health concerns are being found at substantially lower concentrations in England’s rivers.
Concentrations of these so-called ‘forever chemicals’ falling 30% in water and 49% in fish was “brilliant to see,” one researcher told the BBC , saying it was a marker for “how far we have come.”
For many decades, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, have been used to create coatings that resist fire, oil, stains, and water. They’re used in products like waterproof clothing, stain-resistant furniture, food packaging, adhesives, cosmetics, firefighting spray foams, medical equipment, and non-stick cooking surfaces.
All that time, however, PFAS were making their way into the environment where because of their unique structure and characteristics, they substantially resist biodegradation, earning them the moniker ‘forever chemicals.’
Two forms of PFAS known as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid, (PFOS) were banned under the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants in almost all products.
The UK being a party to the convention, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010, and PFOA in 2020. France implemented bans of these two chemicals in certain products in January, while the US Environmental Protection Agency announced new drinking water testing regimes for 6 common PFAS in 2024.
Despite this 10 year disparity, concentrations of PFOA in England’s rivers had still fallen 29% compared to 30% for PFOS in the recent test work conducted by the UK Environment Agency (EA).

The World Health Organization’s Int. Agency for Research on Cancer considers there to be “sufficient” evidence that PFOA is carcinogenic in humans, while research on PFOS suggests this compound is “possibly carcinogenic” in humans.

items.title: For Almost 600 Years, This Enigmatic Jan van Eyck Painting Has Entranced Viewers. Could It Actually Be a Self-Portrait in Disguise?
items.desc: The new theory about the "Arnolfini Portrait" comes as London's National Gallery brings together all 10 of the artist's known portraits for the first time ever
items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
Ahead of a new exhibition celebrating the portraiture of famed Netherlandish painter Jan van Eyck , a new theory has emerged about one of the artist’s most famous—and deeply puzzling—canvases.
At first glance, the scene in van Eyck’s 1434 Arnolfini Portrait seems straightforward: A man, dressed in black, and woman, clad in green, stand at the center of a lavish room where every detail—furniture, a dog, jewelry, oranges—is placed as though to purposefully highlight their wealth. But a closer look at the space’s geometry offers more uncanny observations. There is no fireplace, as would have been expected, and the ceiling is too low to realistically accommodate the chandelier that nonetheless dangles above their heads. Meanwhile, a convex mirror on the far back wall reveals that the pair are not alone; two figures are entering the room. The man in black lifts his hand, apparently in silent greeting, while a large inscription beside his head reads, in Latin: “Jan van Eyck was here 1434.”
Of all the details in the piece, which borders on the surreal, the identity of the man has been speculated upon the most. The leading theory derives from the 16th century, when inventory records labeling the painting as “hernoul le fin” were interpreted to be the French spelling of “Arnoul fin,” or “Arnolfini,” the surname of a wealthy Italian merchant clan who lived and worked in Bruges, Belgium, where van Eyck kept his studio.
For centuries, many art historians have supported this understanding, considering the piece to be a portrait of some members of that family. Some scholars identify the man as Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini, while others think it depicts his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini. But now, as London’s National Gallery prepares to open “ Van Eyck: The Portraits ,” an exhibition, a new theory put forth about the canvas potentially turns its meaning on its head.
Writing in the exhibition catalogue , Stephan Kemperdick , a curator at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie , posits that the painting is actually a self-portrait of van Eyck and his wife. His evidence is multi-faceted. He points to the Latin inscription as a clear self-reference and suggests that “hernoul le fin” actually translates to mean something like “a deceived cheat.” He argues that the painting, in the early modern period, would have been received as more of a lewd genre piece than a portrait. items.text:
Meaning and use of word has become more important in age of AI chatbot, says dictionary
In a world where the line between people and machines is more blurred than ever, Cambridge dictionary has sided with natural intelligence for its word of the year: human.
Breakthroughs in artificial intelligence – led by the arrival of ChatGPT three years ago – have made the question of what it means to be human as vexed as ever, but the dictionary has drawn a firm line with its choice of the word of 2026, defining “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”.
AI advances have spurred questions about whether computers can achieve consciousness, with the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins among those who answered in the affirmative, saying he was “left with the overwhelming feeling that they are human”. Sceptics, on the other hand , argue that there is a vast difference between how a human brain evolves and how an AI system is built.
Cambridge dictionary said the meaning and use of “human” had become more important in the age of the chatbot. Colin McIntosh, an editor of the dictionary, said AI was “changing the way we talk about being human” and had led to the word of the year being deployed to distinguish our work from that of advanced computer systems. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking has made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children,” he said. “A recent increase in compounds such as ‘human-made’ highlight how the word has come to distinguish works or qualities of people, as distinct from AI.”
Prof Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said : “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.”
Other tech-related words were on the shortlist: “agent”, the term for an AI system that can operate – sometimes alarmingly – without human control, and “analogues”, relating to non-digital activities. A non-tech contender was “wholesome”, a word to describe something which is likely to improve your life either physically, morally, or emotionally.

items.title: Government risks missing climate targets if EV rules weakened, adviser warns
items.desc: The UK could miss legally binding climate targets if EV targets are cut, an adviser warns
items.text:
Current rules say all new cars must be zero emission by 2035
The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.
In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".
The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.
The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.
Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.
Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".
Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.
In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.
But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars
SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.
"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.
The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.
The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.

items.text:
Italian artist Marco Martalar transforms discarded branches and reclaimed timber into majestic sculptures that look like they’re straight out of a fantasy film. Many of his majestic creations incorporate trees felled by Storm Vaia, the devastating weather event that swept through large parts of the Italian Alps in 2018.
From a 7-foot-tall sculpture inspired by an ancient water nymph to a gigantic, winged lion, Martalar’s works are a powerful tribute to nature and a celebration of ancient folklore. One of the artist’s most impressive creations is a giant wooden dragon perched on Alpe Cimbra in Lavarone, northern Italy. Made from branches left behind by the storm, the sculpture turns damaged trees into something extraordinary. But the dragon is more than just an impressive work of art. Martalar created it as a symbol of nature’s immense power. He spent 10 days planning the project before dedicating another six weeks to sculpting the creature by hand on site.
Tragically, the original dragon was destroyed by a fire in 2023, leaving little more than ashes behind. But with help from the local community, Martalar brought it back to life. The Vaia Regeneration Drago n was created using six tons of charred wood, with the marks left by the storm and fire becoming part of its form.
Other pieces look like they’ve grown from the earth and could come alive at any second, like The Radicosaur, a unicorn-like creature made in 2025. Martalar describes it as “a peaceful and ancestral creature that, although extremely rare, reveals itself only to children.” According to the artist, the sculpture brings a message of peace and harmony between nature and humans.
Many of Martalar’s works explore themes of resilience and human connection. One example, titled Il Bacio (The Kiss) , stands beside Lake Molveno in northern Italy. The sculpture features two human figures, crafted from weathered wood, facing one another in an intimate pose. Martalar explains (translated), “The work celebrates the silent strength of love, capable of transforming matter into poetry and time into eternity. In that suspended moment, everything is silent: only the universal language of affection remains, which unites living beings like the invisible roots unite the trees of the forest.”

items.title: Conservationists searching for large river eels
items.desc: The Tees Rivers Trust has been searching for eels to tag and track as they migrate out to sea.
items.text:
Tees Rivers Trust workers have been tagging eels to track their downstream migration
Conservationists have spent summer and autumn searching for critically endangered eels to tag as they begin their downstream migration.
The Tees Rivers Trust have found 12 large eels by fyke netting, a method of catching eels with a cylindrical net, around the River Tees catchment.
The team managed to electronically tag 10 of them and the largest was 60cm (23ins) in length and weighted 435g (0.9lbs).
Project manager Ellie Ward said the eels caught this year were not as large as usual and were "harder to catch".
The team has been searching for "silver" eels which have finished maturing and are preparing to head back out to the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda.
Ward said: "European eels start to migrate downstream during autumn and winter, when river discharges increase.
"We suspect that low flows in summer that have continued into autumn have contributed to low catch rates so far this year."
The Eels of Steel project is funded by Natural England and the Tees Rivers Trust has been conducting the research alongside Hull University.
Each eel has a tag which emits a unique ping, which provides information about their movements while migrating.
The project aims to discover if the critically endangered animal is successfully leaving the river and making it through river barriers such as sluices and weirs.
Conservationists say it has been harder than usual to find the eels
Since 2008, European eels have been listed as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Numbers have declined by between 90-95% since the 1980s due to a range of factors including habitat loss, climate change and overfishing.
Ward said: "It is incredible to think about the journey these eels are embarking on, back to their spawning grounds in the Sargasso Sea.
"No-one has ever witnessed European eels spawning, they are a species that hold so much mystery."
The team say they are always open to suggestions for netting locations, particularly lakes and ponds, and ask people to contact them.

items.text:
Most people spend their lives trying to avoid getting arrested, but for one 99-year-old woman in the Netherlands, it was a dream come true. In February 2017, a woman named Annie finally got to check an unusual item off her bucket list, thanks to some accommodating local police officers.
While typical bucket list items might include traveling the world or trying an adventurous activity, Annie had a slightly different goal: experiencing what it was like to be locked up in a jail cell. Luckily, she didn’t have to commit a crime to make it happen.
After learning about her aunt’s unusual wish, Annie’s niece reached out to the police department in Nijmegen-Zuid, Netherlands, to see if they could help. Although civilians aren’t normally allowed inside police holding cells, an officer named Maarten decided to make a special exception.
Annie got the full experience, complete with a ride to the police station, handcuffs, and a brief stay behind bars. And judging by the photos shared online, she couldn’t have been happier. The 99-year-old was all smiles as she posed in handcuffs and waved from inside her cell.
Of course, Annie wasn’t actually in trouble with the law, and the entire experience was arranged just for her. Still, it’s safe to say that she got a taste of life on the other side of the bars, without having to worry about a criminal record.
It just goes to show that you’re never too old to try something new, even if that something happens to be getting arrested.

Georgia O'Keeffe, “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I,” 1930. (Photo: Christie’s Images Ltd. )
You never know what could be hiding in someone’s closet. Earlier this year, a long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting was discovered in the closet of a woman’s Manhattan apartment, and was recently presented as part of Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale in New York.
The 1930 painting, Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I , was estimated to be worth between $3 million and $5 million. On Nov. 17, it sold at auction for $4.8 million. It depicts the tan, green, and brown rolling mountains of New Mexico, using O’Keeffe’s signature sweeping curves that bring the viewer’s eye across the landscape. O’Keeffe first visited New Mexico in 1929 and it would continue to inspire her to paint throughout her career.
“This is a wonderful painting, a remarkable story, and extraordinary opportunity for collectors and the general public alike,” said Tylee Abbott, senior specialist and international director of American Art at Christie’s.
The discovery of the painting itself was just as remarkable. The owner of the work, who wished to remain anonymous, had invited her niece to her East Village apartment earlier this year to help go through her belongings. While the niece knew that her aunt was an art collector, she was shocked when the woman casually mentioned that she had an O’Keeffe in her front closet.
After digging through the closet, her niece found an old wooden box tucked behind dozens of coats. Inside was the 10-inch by 24-inch painting, complete with O’Keeffe’s signature on the original backboard. The painting had been a graduation gift to the owner when she earned her master’s degree in the 1960s. It was purchased by her mother for just $3,800 from O’Keeffe’s art dealer in Manhattan.
The painting hung on the wall of her apartment for over 20 years, until the owner grew worried after noticing that a guest was paying a little too much attention to it. She decided to tuck it away in its original box in the closet, where it remained hidden for decades.
Now, after spending decades out of sight, the painting is finally getting to see the light of day. The work was on public display at Christie’s New York, November 7-17, ahead of its appearance at the auction house’s 20th Century Evening Sale.

items.text:
Capri, Italy, boasts dramatic cliffs, bright blue waters, and sunny Mediterranean weather, making it one of the most alluring tourist destinations in the world. However, this idyllic site has recently made waves around the world for a completely different reason. A double waterspout appeared next to one of Capri’s main attractions, and this rare weather phenomenon was captured on video.
The clip, captured by Massimo Aprea, shows the two swirling columns almost intertwining over the iconic Faraglioni rock formations. The result is a near-optical illusion of a delicate gray arch framing the landscape. Upon closer inspection, one can see the two parallel water pillars descending from the stormy sky and touching the ocean.
A waterspout is a whirling column of air and water mist, as winds blowing from opposite directions slam into each other. In this particular case, cooler winds moved over the warm Mediterranean air as a storm approached. This created localized areas of spinning air on the water’s surface.
Waterspouts are divided into two categories, fair weather waterspouts and tornadic waterspouts. The double one seen in Capri falls onto the latter, meaning they have the same characteristics as a land tornado, and they are usually accompanied by severe thunderstorms, as well as high winds and seas, large hail, and frequent dangerous lightning.
While the double watersprout provided a beautiful natural spectacle, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) says these type of watersprouts can quickly become dangerous, so it’s best to stay out of their way.
“The best way to avoid a waterspout is to move at a 90-degree angle to its apparent movement,” the NOAA states. “Never move closer to investigate a waterspout. Some can be just as dangerous as tornadoes.” The agency adds that if a waterspout moves onshore, the National Weather Service will issue a tornado warning.

items.text:
Rock layers record the Earth’s history, typically piling up from oldest at the bottom to youngest at the top. But a giant, mysterious gap exists in many of the globe’s landmasses. It’s well-documented in North America, northern Europe and northern China, where in some places more than one billion years of our planet’s geologic record is nowhere to be found.
Now, scientists say they may have figured out what caused the so-called Great Unconformity.
Computer simulations hint the missing rock layers, which should be older than roughly 540 million years old, were uplifted by movements of Earth’s viscous mantle layer and eroded away by giant ice sheets before the continents sank back down again. The findings, published November 4 in the journal Nature , help validate some of the possible explanations about the Great Unconformity, possibly solving the 150-year-old mystery.
“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. items.text:
Across ancient Egypt, millions of cats were once mummified and laid to rest in sprawling animal necropolises to honor the gods. Now, a closer look at more than a hundred preserved skulls reveals that these sacred animals endured surprisingly brutal lives.
Researchers analyzed 131 well-preserved cat skulls housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna that originally came from Beni Hassan , an ancient animal funerary site in Egypt’s Nile Valley, some 155 miles south of Cairo. The majority of skulls belonged to adult cats, mostly domestic and some wild. They were largely dated between 380 B.C.E. and 40 B.C.E Osteological and chemical examinations revealed widespread signs of gum disease, infections, healed wounds and fatal skull fractures, according to a study recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science .
“What struck us most was the high proportion of injuries and evidence of disease, suggesting that these cats lived in poor conditions,” Bea De Cupere , study co-author and archaeozoologist at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, tells Phys.org ’s Sandee Oster. “This is not what one would expect for animals destined to become votive mummies.”
In ancient Egypt, cats were revered as earthly embodiments of the goddess Bastet and frequently appeared on tomb walls and artifacts. Eventually, devotees began mummifying felines as sacred offerings across at least 20 animal cemeteries in Egypt, according to the study.

Antarctic blue whales have increased in number 1,000% since 1973 when the harpoons were finally hung up for good.
Growing from just 418 whales to 4,018, the superb recovery has averaged 4.5% per year.
Though the International Whaling Commission banned the killing of Antarctic blue whales in 1964, illegal whaling continued until 1973. These long-lived animals—the largest ever known to have existed—reproduce very slowly with just one calf every 3 years or so.
As impressive a comeback as the whales have made, counting 4,018 animals was also quite the impressive feat of data science.
Even though one can spot a blue whale with a satellite, the Southern Ocean population spends most of its time underwater.
Zoe Rand, a postdoctoral scholar in the University of Washington School of Marine and Environmental Affairs, lead a study that examined historical catch data, modern photo identification records, and decades of “line transect” surveys to estimate current population.
Line transect surveys from 1978 to 1984, 1985 to 1991, and 1991 to 2004 surveyed the entire Southern Ocean by sailing boats along straight lines and counting whales seen and the distances they remained from the boat.
These data sources not only indicated the number was growing, but that it has grown so substantially over time.

Rand wrote in a statement that blue whales and whales in general are marine ecosystem engineers that change vast areas through their activity. During feed, defecation, or death, thousands of other creatures directly respond to blue whale biology.

items.text:
Inquest-style inquiry concludes iron age remains are of 15- to 22-year-old female who may have been ritually sacrificed
A coroner’s investigation into Northern Ireland ’s most venerable cold case has concluded that the victim was decapitated more than 2,000 years ago.
The inquest-style inquiry determined that Ballymacombs More Woman – the name given to iron age remains found in a County Derry bog three years ago – was between 15 and 22 years old when she was beheaded from behind with a bladed weapon.
The inquiry, hosted at the Ulster Museum on Monday, was not a formal inquest but adopted the structure and methodology of a coroner’s investigation and drew on the latest archaeological, forensic and scientific evidence to examine the death.
“The purpose of the exercise is not to impose modern legal conclusions upon the distant past, but to provide a framework through which the available evidence could be assessed and the story of a previously unknown young woman could be told,” said the coroner for Northern Ireland , Joe McCrisken, who chaired the investigation.
“Although separated from us by more than 20 centuries, she was once a living member of her community, and the investigation sought to restore, insofar as possible, an understanding of her life, death and place in history.”
The precise circumstances surrounding the woman’s death remain unknown, but evidence suggests it was part of a tradition of ritualised killing and sacrifice documented among other iron age bodies discovered across north-western Europe.
“What we have learned from this detailed research has allowed us to share her story with clarity and confidence,” said Hannah Crowdy, the head of curatorial at National Museums NI. “She has provided a significant insight into the iron age, and how we as a society have evolved over time.”
Peat workers discovered the remains in a bog in the townland of Ballymacombs More outside Bellaghy in October 2023, leading to an archaeological excavation which uncovered bones – though no skull – and a woven artefact.

items.text:
A Catholic health care system in the American Midwest has successfully completed the world’s first reported bone marrow transplant to treat a non-malignant disease.
Doctors at Franciscan Health used bone marrow recovered from a deceased organ donor to treat a 40-year-old woman with aplastic anemia
The patient, with a decade-long history of the disease, received the bone marrow stem cell transplant on April 18, after her disease progressed from stable to severe, despite multiple lines of therapy.
Because her disease no longer responded to medication, her care team pursued a transplant to replace her failing marrow with healthy blood-forming stem cells.
Six months after the transplant, the donor marrow has taken hold and restored her blood counts.
She no longer needs blood or platelet transfusions and has achieved full donor chimerism, meaning her blood and immune system are now produced entirely by the donor’s stem cells, without complications.
For non-malignant conditions including severe aplastic anemia, sickle cell disease, beta thalassemia, and other inherited or acquired bone marrow failure disorders, bone marrow-derived stem cells are widely regarded as the preferred stem cell source over peripheral blood stem cells (PBSCs), and the source of choice for non-malignant diseases.
“Bone marrow transplantation for severe aplastic anemia has been performed since the 1970s using living related and unrelated donors.
“To our knowledge, this is the first reported transplant of deceased organ donor bone marrow for severe aplastic anemia,” said Felix Mensah, MD, the treating physician at Franciscan Health.
“This case shows why continued innovation in transplant medicine matters, and why we need more donor options, so that every patient with a life-threatening bone marrow failure disorder has access to potentially curative therapy.”
“Reaching the first non-malignant transplant is a defining moment,” said Kevin Caldwell , Co-Founder and CEO of Ossium, which maintains a marrow bank.
“By recovering and banking bone marrow from organ donors, we can consistently optimize treatment outcomes.”

A pill that mimics Viagra by relaxing blood vessels and increasing blood flow to the brain can slow cognitive decline in people with Alzheimer’s disease by almost a third, a global study suggests.
Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, a condition that is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050. There is currently no cure.
In a stage three trial spanning 13 countries, including the UK, researchers found the tablet AR1001 slowed decline by 31% in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease not receiving any other treatment.

items.title: The Bloomsbury Group's Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant Tangled Their Art and Lives Together for Decades. A Final Sketch of Bell on Her Deathbed Just Resurfaced After 60 Years
items.desc: The two artists had a thoroughly complicated relationship—and a daughter—but never ceased to paint and draw each other. The new discovery points to an artistic bond that continued through health and sickness
items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
The lives of artists Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell —collaborators, companions and sometimes lovers—were deeply intertwined both on canvases and in private quarters.
The pair were central figures in the Bloomsbury Group , a circle of artists and intellectuals active in early 20th-century Britain who radically, and often controversially, challenged contemporary creative and social norms. These included public sentiments on philosophy, sexuality and mental illness. The group featured, among others, the economist John Maynard Keynes , as well as the writers E. M. Forster and Virginia Woolf , Bell’s biological sister.
Grant and Bell were often the subjects of each other’s work. Among their most well-known collaborations is one of Grant’s first and most extravagant depictions of Bell, a full-length portrait painted in 1915.
But this summer, while preparing for “ Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury ,” an exhibition that opened this week at Tate Britain, scholars discovered an intimate, previously unknown work that sheds new light on the end of Grant and Bell’s relationship.
Hidden for some 60 years among private family papers, the newly recovered drawing is thought to be Grant’s final depiction of Bell. Created in an uncharacteristically simple style—soft monochrome pencil and biro on paper—the piece shows an ailing Bell with her eyes closed, head resting on a pillow, from the perspective of an artist who likely was sitting at her bedside. In the bottom right-hand corner, Grant dated the piece April 14, 1961—one week after Bell succumbed to an illness at the age of 81, and two days after her burial.

items.title: From a Small Island in Denmark, This Man Lived Through the Transition From Hunter-Gathering to Farming 6,000 Years Ago
items.desc: A new analysis of the Rødhals Man suggests he witnessed the Neolithic Revolution in his lifetime, growing up eating mostly foraged seafood before shifting to more land-based, likely farmed, foods as an adult
items.text:
Archaeologists have identified a man who likely lived through the shift from hunter-gathering to farming, a dramatic transition that reshaped human history and ultimately paved the way for modern society as we know it.
Researchers have uncovered new details about the diet, lifestyle and health of the “Rødhals Man,” an indigenous hunter-gatherer who lived some 6,000 years ago in what is now Denmark. The findings, published November 16 in the journal Antiquity , suggest the Rødhals Man witnessed the Neolithic agricultural revolution and seemingly found a way to co-exist with farmers.
Rødhals Man is the name given to a near-complete skeleton discovered in 1956 in a shell midden—essentially, an ancient trash dump—on the small Danish island of Sejerø .
For years, researchers were perplexed by the remains. Radiocarbon dating suggested the man was alive between 3900 B.C.E. and 3800 B.C.E., after Neolithic farmers had already begun arriving on the nearby island of Zealand , and lived during a time when people were starting to eat mostly land-based foods grown and raised by farmers. But his DNA revealed that his ancestry was entirely indigenous—he belonged to the Western Hunter-Gatherer genetic group—and his diet consisted primarily of seafood .
“There was something wrong and it is always when things don’t fit that you may be on the track of something important,” lead author Anders Fischer , an archaeologist at the University of Gothenburg, tells New Scientist ’s Chris Simms.
So, researchers decided to take another look at the remains. Their analysis revealed that the Rødhals Man was between 30 and 40 years old when he died—probably closer to the upper end of this range, based on degenerative changes to his body. In life, he stood roughly five feet tall and was right-handed. He had black hair and dark skin, and there’s a very high likelihood his eyes were blue.
The Rødhals Man shows no signs of having experienced violence, and he appears to have been healthy during the early part of his life. Later, as he aged, he developed inflammation or a vitamin deficiency.
An investigation of his teeth and bones revealed that his diet changed over the course of his life. As a child, he mostly ate creatures like mollusks, flatfish or eels, which he likely foraged from the shallow waters surrounding the island. Starting around age 11, however, he began to eat more land-based protein, in addition to seafood.

How much sleep do you get each night? According to the National Center for Health Statistics , one-third of American adults sleep less than seven hours a night—the amount of shuteye recommended by health authorities. Recognizing that many people, particularly students, struggle to get the rest they need, researchers recently explored whether offering small, financial rewards could encourage students to improve their sleeping habits.
The study, published in July 2026, was conducted by Osea Giuntella, associate professor of economics at the University of Pittsburgh; Sally Sadoff, professor of economics and strategy at the University of California, San Diego; and Silvia Saccardo, professor of social and decision sciences at Carnegie Mellon University.
The researchers gave more than 1,100 undergraduates at University of Pittsburgh a Fitbit, a wearable activity tracker that recorded how much they slept, and an app that sent bedtime reminders and morning feedback. They randomly chose 468 freshman students and paid them around $5 for every night they slept at least seven hours over the course of four weeks.
Before the study, students at the University of Pittsburgh were getting an average of just 6.6 hours of sleep a night. “Half were going to bed after 1 a.m. on average—a quarter after 2 a.m,” reveal the researchers. “They also did not know how much sleep they were getting. Two-thirds told us they usually slept seven hours—the trackers showed only about one-third of students slept that much on even three nights out of five.”
Students offered money for getting enough sleep reached the seven hour target on 26% more nights than those who weren’t paid. They also got an extra 19 minutes of sleep each school night—about the difference between closing your laptop at 11:40 p.m. instead of midnight. Getting more sleep seemed to pay off in the classroom, too. Students who received the incentives saw their GPA rise by around 0.08 points that semester. The boost to grades didn’t last forever though, and lowered after two semesters.
The researchers also learned that students who were paid nightly slept more than those who received a lump sum at the end of the semester. Interestingly, bedtime reminders alone made little difference. Students already wanted more sleep—they just needed a little extra incentive to make it happen.

81 years ago today, UNESCO was first formed to promote world peace by uniting countries through education, the arts, sciences, and culture. Fostering universal respect for all nations, UNESCO (which stands for United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) has 193 member states sponsoring projects that improve literacy, provide technical training and education, advance science, and preserve regional and cultural history. UNESCO’s largest and most well-known activity is the designation of landmarks that hold cultural or natural importance. These UNESCO World Heritage Sites are masterpieces of human creative genius and landmarks of nature. Designated as ‘patrimony’, with outstanding value to the story of humanity, there have been 1,223 sites protected across 168 countries, so far. Italy is the country with the UNESCO World Heritage Sites (60) with China closely following with 59—and Germany some distance behind at 54. The United States has 26, many of which are natural.

items.text:
Olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings saved from an approaching storm in California were released into the wild over the weekend.
It was late September when a female turtle climbed out of the sea, dug a nest on the beach, deposited her clutch, and slipped back into the water leaving nothing but a small trail in the sand and a couple of speechless lifeguards.
This first-ever instance of a turtle nesting on America’s Pacific coast was repeated a day later on Huntington Beach in what were the first ever recorded sea turtle nests on the West Coast.
After at first being left to incubate and hatch naturally, storm forecasts saw state and federal authorities evacuate the nests and take the eggs to the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach.
The hatchlings emerged at the Aquarium and were quickly transported to Orange County beaches for release. Photos released by the Aquarium that were taken with red or infrared light show handlers measuring each hatchling before letting them scurry down to the water on their own, with minimal human disturbance and other distractions.
“It is not known why these sea turtles chose Southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it may indicate important historical changes that could have long-term implications for this species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” said Cassandra Davis, Director of Volunteer Services at the Aquarium, who said neither weather nor mere anomalous behavior were being ruled out as a theory.
Jonathan Snyder of the US Fish and Wildlife Service office in Carlsbad said another nest was recently documented further up the coast in Ventura County in November, and that it’s therefore unclear exactly how many turtles have nested in total.
He told reporters that one obvious potential reason for this never-before-witnessed event could be the Super El Niño weather phenomenon this year, though his overarching thoughts were positive.
“There have been decades of effort by dedicated individuals both in the US and abroad that have done everything they can for sea turtle conservation, and those efforts have really moved the needle for conservation for a variety of species, but for Olive Ridley sea turtles in particular,” said Snyder in a press conference.
“Their populations have increased substantially throughout portions of their range, and it’s the reason why there are these sea turtles along our coast that could take advantage of these unique environmental conditions.”

items.title: A Child Tossed a Hat, and a Ceiling Fan Sent It Flying Into a Hippo's Zoo Enclosure, Where the Animal Ate It. Here's How the Care Team Is Responding
items.desc: The Cincinnati Zoo’s beloved hippo Fiona is under constant medical surveillance, but her carers are “cautiously optimistic” that she will pass the object on her own and recover
items.text:
Carlyn Kranking | Associate Web Editor, Science
It was an almost impossible series of events. At the Cincinnati Zoo, a child tossed a knit cap into the air, where a ceiling fan caught it and sent it flying to the side. The hat sailed through a one-foot opening above 12-foot-high viewing windows in Fiona the hippo’s enclosure. The animal ingested the item.
“We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried,” Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, says in a statement to Casey Weldon and Kristen Swilley of Axios .
The incident, which occurred earlier this month, was an accident, the zoo states. Now, the veterinary and hippo care teams are monitoring Fiona around the clock and working to help her pass the object. They’ve given her fluids and an enema, as well as medications to reduce nausea and act like laxatives.
“We know from consulting with specialists … that surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos,” Mike Wenninger , director of animal health at the Cincinnati Zoo, said in a video update on Tuesday. “Our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she can pass this on her own.”
On Monday, the team wrote that they are “cautiously optimistic” on Facebook . “We know how much Fiona means to so many of you.”
Fiona became widely beloved in 2017 after she was born six weeks prematurely , weighing just 29 pounds , instead of the average 55 to 120 pounds. In multiple tube feedings each day , caretakers gave her a custom milk formula, and they used an IV catheter to deliver fluids. The public followed eagerly along as she took her shaky first steps and recovered, and Fiona gained a base of lifelong fans. She even inspired a book and a line of beer .
Fiona, currently 9 years old, has a younger brother named Fritz who was born at the Cincinnati Zoo in August 2022 . His birth inspired an ice cream flavor .
A few days after ingesting the hat, Fiona’s appetite started to decrease. This week, her care team ran diagnostics again and repeated fluid therapy to promote her hydration. They borrowed a nine-foot scope from the Columbus Zoo to conduct a colonoscopy, but they couldn’t reach the hat in her digestive tract. An ultrasound suggested the hippo’s small intestine is bunching, as if she is passing something through it.
“At this point, what we can do is supportive care,” Wenninger said in the video. “We’re trying to give her all of her favorite foods and try to get her to keep passing things through.”

items.desc: "The Book of Miracles," a 16th-century manuscript likely created in Augsburg, is heading to auction. It features 167 paintings of extreme weather events and strange celestial phenomena
items.text:
Ellen Wexler | Writer and Special Projects Editor
In the Bible, God’s will often emerges through natural phenomena. The great flood cleanses the earth of human corruption, while the rainbow symbolizes the divine covenant “between God and every living creature.” For millennia, worshippers familiar with these stories have wondered: What meaning can be found in the movements of storms, seas and stars?
That’s the central question of The Book of Miracles , an illustrated manuscript dating to the mid-16th century. Featuring 167 imaginative paintings, the text begins with episodes from the Old Testament and ends with apocalyptic visions from the Book of Revelation . Between them is a catalog of earthquakes , comet sightings , locust plagues , volcanic eruptions and other events spanning antiquity through the manuscript’s creation.
Now, The Book of Miracles is heading to the auction block, where it’s expected to fetch between roughly $920,000 and $1.3 million. Bidders can vie for the volume during Christie’s Valuable Books and Manuscripts sale on December 10.
“The artists of The Book of Miracles have reinterpreted historical and contemporary sources with apocalyptic panache,” per the lot listing . Illustrations of earthquakes, floods and other natural disasters that occurred in Europe are “among the most energetic, imaginative and colorful illustrations in the manuscript.”
The text was rediscovered in the library of a Bavarian castle about two decades ago. It’s since changed hands several times. After acquiring the manuscript, London art dealer James Faber helped date it to the 16th century. The publisher Taschen released a facsimile edition in 2013.
Because The Book of Miracles depicts about a dozen events near Augsburg , a city in modern-day Germany, scholars think it may have been created there. Christie’s attributes the manuscript to two painters, Hans Burgkmair the Younger and Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger , and their workshops. It was a sight which struck terror into the firefighters called to tackle it - a blazing chemical waste lagoon on fire, with barrels exploding into the air.
Steve Williams, then in his 20s, was one of 60 firefighters sent to tackle the burning Llwyneinion lagoon in August 1980, which was sending thick black smoke over a nearby village.

"It's a definite probability," said the 71-year-old. "They're firemen and they're always running into fires, so you don't know what the long-term effects are going to be - but actually falling into the lake and drinking that fluid, which is full of chemicals. He had a double-whammy, didn't he?"

items.desc: People installing their own solar panels has helped boost the solar share of Pakistan's electricity from 1% to 28%.
items.text:
Faizal Shahzad wants to buy several more solar panels to make his home in rural Punjab fully self-sufficient
Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.
But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.
"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."
Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.
From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.
People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."
Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.
This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eﬀects.
The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.
Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".
"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."

People visiting a large illuminated sculpture of the Moon have said it is an "amazing" sight.
ArtHouse Jersey has brought Luke Jerram's artwork to the St Helier Methodist Centre until Sunday 29 November.
The 6m (20ft) wide display, which has been shown around the world, features detailed imagery of the lunar surface from photographs by Nasa.
Arthouse CEO Tom Dingle said: "Something that makes the most of a public space, that makes us think about the world around us, about ourselves, but also something that we can all share together all at once, is really exciting."
Eva, nine, said it was "cool" to see a sculpture of the Moon up close
The Moon follows a similar public artwork display in Jersey in 2023, when more than 31,000 people visited the Floating Earth on Queen's Valley Reservoir .
The installation features light and sound displays, which ArtHouse said would allow people "to encounter our closest celestial neighbour in an entirely new way".
Nine-year-old Eva thought the moon was "cool" and "like a big spot in the middle of the sky".
Primrose Keenan also enjoyed the exhibit, saying it was "amazing".
"We saw the Earth on the lake as well a few couple of years ago and that was amazing too," she added.
Toby Balderson said: "It does make a difference being able to see everything in such detail.
"We always just see little snapshots of it."
Youngsters Aquila and Starla, who are sisters, said it looked "really good" and "very big".
Dingle added: "Sometimes to stop, to take a pause and to reflect on the wider things, to think about the world out there, is actually really healthy and therapeutic."
He said the exhibit also showed the importance of free public artwork: "It enlivens our public realm, it gives us something to do together.
"It actually can change the pace for a day. It can give somebody a moment to reflect and it can mean something different to everybody - and yet we have the same universal experience at the same time."

What began as an exciting hiking trip quickly turned into something else entirely when climbers in Greece found an orphaned seal pup on a beach at the bottom of a cliff.
Considered a Critically Endangered species in Greece, the climbers resolved to go right back up the way they came—the seal pup safely secured in a backpack.
It was stranded without its mother on the inaccessible Kalamia Beach—whose beauty and solitude were supposed to be the climbers’ reward for negotiating the rugged cliffs on the island of Kythira.
Vrettos Sklavos, from Outdoor Activities Greece said there is a sea cave near Kalamia Beach that these Mediterranean monk seals use to escape rough seas. Perhaps a big wave had separated the little fellow from its mother.
An animal rescue operation on the island wrote on Facebook that the climbers took “all the right steps,” calling (MOm) the Hellenic Society for the Study and Protection of the Mediterranean Monk Seal, the coast guard, and Animal Aid Kythira , whose veterinarians eventually descended the cliffs together with the climbers to rescue the seal.
“A huge thank you to Vrettos and his team for their immediate response,” the operation wrote on Facebook.
In an update from Keep Talking Greece , the seal is said to have arrived severely dehydrated and malnourished, weighing just 15 kilograms at 1 year old. It was determined that after a brief stay with Animal Aid Kythira it would be transported to Thessaly on the mainland before eventually arriving at the Society’s rehabilitation location in Spata.
Here, it will receive round-the-clock care with the aim of attempting to preserve enough of its wild intuition and nature as to permit a return to the sea when the time is right.

items.title: These Adorable Hatchlings Are From the U.S. West Coast's First Known Natural Sea Turtle Nests. Now, They've Returned to the Wild
items.desc: Two nests were spotted in September, and authorities moved the eggs to an aquarium to protect them from an incoming tropical storm. Over the weekend, dozens of hatchlings emerged and have now been released on the same beaches where they were found
items.text:
In September, authorities in California were baffled to find two sea turtle nests on their beaches—the first natural ones ever confirmed on the United States’ West Coast. Now, dozens of the eggs have hatched. Experts released the baby olive ridley turtles over the weekend, allowing the tiny creatures to begin their perilous journeys to adulthood.
The two nests were identified on Seal Beach and Huntington Beach in Orange County. Because a tropical storm was coming soon after the nests were found, biologists moved the more than 200 eggs to the Aquarium of the Pacific. The Ping-Pong ball-size spheres stayed in closed incubators under sand in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room, simulating their ideal natural conditions.
Aquarium staff first saw signs of hatching activity on November 12, when they noticed changes in the surface of the sand in the incubation container with the Seal Beach eggs, said Lance Adams , the aquarium’s veterinarian, during a press conference on November 14. The team spotted a depression and some cracks in the sand, indicating something was happening beneath it. The first turtle emerged the following day at around 7:15 p.m. Pacific time. Around two hours later, more of the baby turtles from the Seal Beach nest started popping out, resulting in 54 squirming critters.
“It kind of went from looking like very smooth beach sand to looking like an eruption of baby sea turtles,” Adams explained. It “was really exciting and very, very cute.” As of the press conference date, 50 eggs from the nest had not hatched. Experts do not know whether they’re viable, but they will continue monitoring the makeshift home.
The Seal Beach hatchlings were released in the same location where their nest had been, very early on Saturday morning, before the sun had risen, according to a social media post . That’s because baby turtles use moonlight to navigate toward the ocean. After reaching the water, hatchlings experience a “frenzy period” in which they swim continuously for 24 to 48 hours, according to the post. The energetic outburst is justified; experts estimate that only one in 1,000 olive ridley turtle hatchlings survive to adulthood, according to a statement .

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA 's Voyager 1 probe , which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.
While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and " Solar System Family Portrait " images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.
One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter . From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system 's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA . As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.
A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.
Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.
Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes , which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

items.title: Chihuahuas Seem to Carry a Tiny Bit of Coyote DNA—but That's Probably Not Why They Have Fearless Personalities
items.desc: New research suggests that coyote DNA makes up about 0.1 percent of the Chihuahua genome, likely the result of interbreeding between coyotes and the domesticated dog's ancestors long ago
items.text:
Thousands of years ago, the ancestors of Chihuahuas mated with wild coyotes. Today, traces of that ancient interbreeding live on in the DNA of the popular pint-size dogs—but they likely aren’t responsible for the creatures’ fearless personalities.
A study published in July in the journal Nature Communications has found a sliver of coyote DNA buried in the Chihuahua genome, their complete set of genetic material. Researchers don’t know exactly when coyote DNA entered the tiny pooch’s gene pool, but their findings suggest the genetic link arose long ago, before Europeans arrived in the Americas.
Scientists made this discovery by accident. They were testing a new high-resolution, genomic ancestry software algorithm and decided to include the DNA of three Chihuahuas, plus numerous other canid breeds and species.
“The genetic calling cards found in the Chihuahua are unmistakably coyote,” study co-author Alexander Ioannidis , a geneticist at Stanford University, tells the New York Times ’ Franz Lidz.
Researchers weren’t necessarily surprised by this result. Past evidence has suggested that dogs and coyotes interbred in the Americas before the arrival of Europeans. However, this is the first time scientists have found genetic traces of that interbreeding in modern dogs, Adam Boyko , a canine geneticist at Cornell University who was not involved with the new work, tells the Times .
Chihuahuas are believed to have descended from the Techichi, a now-extinct, mute breed kept by the Toltec civilization in what is now Mexico as early as the 9th century C.E. About 4 percent of the Chihuahua genome comes from the Techichi. Within that 4 percent, an even smaller fraction comes from the coyote.
In total, researchers estimate that coyote DNA makes up roughly 0.1 percent of the entire Chihuahua genome. Unfortunately for anyone hoping to pin the pooch’s big personality on its wild ancestry, this tiny amount of coyote DNA probably hasn’t influenced the breed’s temperament, the scientists say.
The team also found identical segments of coyote DNA in the Chinese crested , a close evolutionary relative of the Chihuahua. This suggests the genetic material entered the dogs’ family tree long ago, through interbreeding between coyotes and an ancient breed—possibly the barkless Techichi—that eventually gave rise to both modern breeds. But researchers say they need to conduct additional genomic research to confirm this idea.

Mexico is one of the leading countries in automobile manufacturing. However, the bulk of this industry is built around American, Asian, and European companies, as 90% of vehicles manufactured in Mexico are exported. A new endeavor wants to take a different approach for this sector, developing its own technology rather than just assembling cars for others. Mexico is now launching Olinia , its own national electric vehicle brand.
The name Olinia comes from the Nahuatl word meaning “to move” or “movement,” as a nod to Mexico’s Indigenous heritage and the desire to put Mexico in the driver’s seat. Tasked with addressing the mobility needs for large areas of Mexico with an accessible, efficient, and sustainable approach, Olinia has enlisted top talents from around the country, integrating engineering, software, design, manufacturing, and services under one umbrella.
Rather than competing with major car brands, Olinia just aims to help locals with their day-to-day tasks, such as carrying groceries or picking the kids up from school. With these short trips in mind, their vehicles can reach a maximum speed of 50 kilometers (31 miles) per hour. But that doesn’t make it less powerful; its 13.5-kilowatt (kW) electric motor is capable of climbing hills and remaining reliable in the rain thanks to its water-resistant capabilities.
So far, two models of Olinia vehicles have been introduced. First up is Olinia Uno , which can carry up to six people. It even has enough space to accommodate one person in a wheelchair.
